newsitem.title: UK: Decade after Bhopal breathing problems persist.
newsitem.headline: Decade after Bhopal breathing problems persist.

text.p: More than a decade after the world's worst industrial disaster in Bhopal, India many local people are still suffering from breathing problems, researchers reported on Friday.
Up to 6,500 people were killed after 27 tonnes of toxic gas leaked from a pesticide factory owned by American multinational Union Carbide and dispersed over the city on December 3, 1984.

Researchers from Britain and the United States who examined residents in Bhopal more than 10 years after the accident found that respiratory symptoms were more common and lung function was reduced among people who were exposed to the gas.
They also discovered that the nearer the people lived to the gas leak site, the more they suffered from respiratory symptoms.

"The frequency of symptoms fell as exposure decreased, as estimated by distance lived from the plant, and lung function measurements displayed similar trends," Paul Cullinan, a senior lecturer at Imperial College in London said in a report in the British Medical Journal.
"Our results suggest that persistent small airways obstruction among survivors of the 1984 disaster may be attributed to gas exposure," he added.

Cullinan and other members of the International Medical Commission on Bhopal studied a random sample of 454 adults in Bhopal. They found that 54 percent of people who were exposed to the gas said they had a cough and 15 percent reported coughing phlegm for at least three months each year.
More than 84 percent said they had difficulty breathing and nine percent said they wheezed in the past 12 months.
The team said their findings suggested that further, locally initiated studies were needed, as well as controlled trials of effective treatments.

In an accompanying commentary in the BMJ, Paul Garner, head of the international health division of the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine said industry has a responsibility to protect the public and a lot more can be done to reduce occupational and local environmental risks.

"Any organisation promoting or participating in economic development in poor countries has a moral responsibility to ensure they do not risk the health of the majority for the benefit of a few," he said.
